summary.text: Empirical probability, also called experimental probability, is an estimate of how likely an event is, made from observed outcomes rather than a theoretical sample space.
A common estimate is the relative frequency: the number of recorded outcomes of the event divided by the total number of trials.
It is relatively free of assumptions, but probabilities very close to zero or one need very large samples to be estimated well.

facts.label: Common estimator
facts.value: Relative frequency: event outcomes over total trials

facts.label: Weak spot
facts.value: Probabilities very close to zero or one

items.prompt: You toss a thumbtack 50 times and it lands point-up 18 times. What is your empirical estimate that it lands point-up?

options.label: 18 out of 50
50 out of 18
1 out of 2
18 out of 32

items.explain: The empirical probability is estimated as the relative frequency: the number of outcomes in which the event occurs over the total number of trials.

items.prompt: You want the share of men who are over 6 feet tall and also prefer strawberry jam. Which approach needs no assumption about how those two traits relate?

options.label: Multiplying the two separate shares together
Assuming the two traits are linked in some way
Counting the men who satisfy both conditions
Guessing from the share of men over 6 feet alone

items.explain: Directly counting men who meet both conditions gives the empirical probability, while multiplying the shares relies on the assumption that the conditions are statistically independent.

items.prompt: A factory wants the chance of a defect that almost never happens. Why are simple counts a poor tool here?

options.label: Counts always give exactly zero
Counting is banned for rare events
Rare events cannot be observed
Very large samples would be needed for good accuracy

items.explain: For probabilities very close to zero or one, very large sample sizes are needed to estimate them to a good standard of relative accuracy.

items.prompt: In past records, a site's coldest February daily high has never gone below zero degrees Celsius. How could someone still estimate the chance it does?

options.label: Fit a family of distributions to the past values
Assume that it can never happen
Wait until it happens before estimating
Count only the years with a freeze

items.explain: A fitted distribution can give an estimate of the probability even if all the values in the record are greater than zero.

items.prompt: What do we call an estimate of a probability that is not based on any observations but on deductive reasoning?

options.label: A relative frequency
An experimental probability
An a priori probability
An empirical probability

items.explain: An a priori probability is an estimate not based on any observations but on deductive reasoning, in contrast to the empirical or a-posteriori kind.

items.prompt: A student sees relative frequency called a-posteriori probability and assumes it is the same thing as a Bayesian posterior probability. Is that right?

options.label: Yes, they are two names for one idea
No, the phrase is not directly related to Bayesian inference
Yes, but only for large samples
No, a-posteriori has no meaning in statistics

items.explain: Though the term recalls Bayesian statistics, a-posteriori probability in this sense is not directly related to Bayesian inference, where posterior probability is different.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Empirical probability, also called experimental probability, is an estimate of how likely an event is. It comes from an actual sample of observations rather than from a theoretical sample space. More broadly, it can be estimated from experience and observation.

paragraphs.heading: How to work it out
paragraphs.text: The usual way to estimate it is the relative frequency. Count how many times the event was recorded, then divide by the total number of trials. In symbols, if an event A in a sample space happens in m outcomes out of n outcomes in all, its relative frequency is m/n.

paragraphs.heading: Strength: few assumptions
paragraphs.text: One advantage of this approach is that it rests on relatively few assumptions. Suppose you want the chance that a man is over 6 feet tall and also prefers strawberry jam to raspberry jam. You could simply count the men who meet both conditions. Another route would multiply the share of men over 6 feet by the share who prefer strawberry jam, but that estimate depends on assuming the two traits are statistically independent.

paragraphs.heading: Weakness: near-zero or near-one odds
paragraphs.text: Trouble comes with probabilities very close to zero or very close to one. Estimating those to a good standard of relative accuracy would need very large samples. Statistical models can help here, depending on the context, and may give better accuracy than empirical probabilities, as long as the assumptions behind them actually hold.

paragraphs.heading: Example: a freezing February
paragraphs.text: Suppose you want the probability that, at some site, the lowest of the daily-maximum temperatures in February of a given year drops below zero degrees Celsius. You could use the record of past years to estimate it. Alternatively, you could pick a family of probability distributions, fit it to the past values, and take the probability from the fitted distribution. The model route can give an answer even if every value in the record is above zero.

paragraphs.heading: Other names
paragraphs.text: It is sometimes called a-posteriori probability. That name echoes terms from Bayesian statistics, yet it has no direct link to Bayesian inference, where a similar-sounding term can mean posterior probability, which is a different thing. In the empirical sense, a-posteriori probability may be paired with a priori probability, an estimate built on deductive reasoning rather than on observations.
